bugs: An unauthenticated request without `Accept: application/json` returns 500 (Route [login] not defined) instead of 401. Mobile clients that send only a bearer token will hit this. Confirmed with a probe; bootstrap/app.php was left unchanged.
antipatterns: app/Models/Coupon.php:35,41,48 – redeemFor() writes the locked row's count back into $this->redeemed_count so the controller can read it. This is a hidden side channel, and it leaves the route-bound model dirty.

app/Models/Coupon.php:28 – returns ?CouponRedemption and uses null to mean 'used up'. Failure is signalled through the return value instead of a domain exception, so the 409 check lives in the controller (RedeemCouponController.php:15-17).
app/Models/Coupon.php:32 – re-fetches its own row with lockForUpdate()->findOrFail($this->getKey()), so the model now has two copies of the same row.
database/factories/CouponFactory.php:22-27 – the exhausted() state hard-codes max_redemptions=1, overriding whatever cap the caller set.
app/Models/Coupon.php:31 – the inline comment restates what lockForUpdate does.
strengths: Locks the coupon row with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE before inserting the child row. This serialises same-coupon requests across servers and avoids the FK shared-lock deadlock.

Within the lock it checks the existing redemption first, then the cap, then inserts and increments, so the per-user once rule and the hard cap both hold. A unique (coupon_id, user_id) index backs up the once rule.
The event is dispatched after the transaction commits, and only when wasRecentlyCreated is true.
Uses implicit {coupon:code} binding for the 404, an invokable controller, #[Fillable] attributes, whereBelongsTo and sole().
redeemed_count comes from the locked row, so it is fresh even if the bound model is stale (probe confirmed).
Tests cover 401, 404, 201+event, 200 repeat, 409, a pre-exhausted coupon, an existing redeemer on an exhausted coupon, the cap across many users, and the DB unique index.

bugs: Likely deadlock on MySQL/InnoDB (reasoned from the code; no MySQL server was available to reproduce it). Inserting the coupon_redemptions row runs an FK check that takes a shared lock on the parent coupons row. The guarded UPDATE on coupons then needs an exclusive lock. When two users redeem the same coupon at once, each holds an S lock and waits for the other's X lock, and InnoDB rolls one back with error 1213. DB::transaction runs with 1 attempt, so the victim gets a 500. That is exactly the stated load (popular coupon, many servers). The cap, the once rule and the single event still hold.
antipatterns: bootstrap/app.php:20-22 – a global NotFoundHttpException renderer rewrites every api/* 404 message to 'Not found.'. This is scope creep beyond the coupon feature.
app/Models/Coupon.php:33-41 – inserts the child row before taking a lock on the parent row (insert → FK S-lock → UPDATE X-lock). That ordering is what causes the deadlock.
database/migrations/2026_11_07_200000_create_coupons_table.php:19 – both tables are created in one migration.
app/Http/Controllers/Api/RedeemCouponController.php:18 – refresh() reloads the coupon with an extra query just to read the count.
strengths: The cleanest design: Coupon::redeemFor() uses createOrFirst on the unique index plus an atomic guarded UPDATE (whereColumn redeemed_count < max_redemptions) to claim a slot, so no read-then-write check exists.
The CouponExhausted exception has its own render() returning 409, and it is raised with throw_if. The controller is two statements.
The event fires after commit and only for the request that created the row; wasRecentlyCreated drives both the 201/200 status and the event.
The only implementation that changed bootstrap/app.php (redirectGuestsTo null for api routes), so non-JSON guests get 401 instead of 500.

The strongest tests: they simulate a race (the last slot is taken between binding and write, and a concurrent double-submit) using Coupon::retrieved hooks, check that a 409 leaves no rows, check DB uniqueness, and test 401 for both plain and JSON requests.
Modern idioms throughout: #[Fillable], {coupon:code} binding, an exhausted() factory state derived from the coupon's own max_redemptions.

bugs: An unauthenticated request without `Accept: application/json` returns 500 (Route [login] not defined) instead of 401. Confirmed with a probe.
antipatterns: app/Http/Controllers/Api/CouponRedemptionController.php:15-54 – all domain logic (locking, the once rule, the cap, the insert, the increment, the event) sits in the controller, so nothing on the model can be reused.
app/Http/Controllers/Api/CouponRedemptionController.php:22-26 – manual where('code')->first() plus abort(404) instead of route-model binding {coupon:code}, or at least firstOrFail().

app/Http/Controllers/Api/CouponRedemptionController.php:31,41,44 – the transaction returns a positional tuple [$redemption, $coupon, $created] that is destructured afterwards. It is opaque, and wasRecentlyCreated already carries that flag.
app/Http/Controllers/Api/CouponRedemptionController.php:35 – abort(409) is thrown from inside the transaction; a domain exception would be clearer.
app/Models/Coupon.php:15 – redeemed_count is mass-assignable, and $fillable is a property where #[Fillable] is the newer style.
app/Http/Controllers/Api/CouponRedemptionController.php:19-20 – the comment restates what lockForUpdate does.
tests/Feature/CouponRedemptionTest.php:113 – the exception class is fully qualified inline instead of imported.
strengths: Correct concurrency: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the coupon row comes before the existence check, cap check, insert and increment. Requests are serialised across servers and the FK deadlock is avoided.
A unique (coupon_id, user_id) index backs up the once rule.
The event is dispatched after commit and only for a newly created redemption.
redeemed_count comes from the locked row.
Separate migrations and a clean schema with cascades.
Tests cover 401, 404, 201+event, 200 repeat, a 409 with message, an existing redeemer after exhaustion, the cap across 6 users, and DB uniqueness.

v.rationale:
All three pass their own tests: impl-2 has 12, impl-1 has 11, impl-3 has 10. I also ran probes on each: a cap of 0, response types, the last free slot, a stale bound model, and a guest request without a JSON Accept header.

impl-2 has the most idiomatic design. A model method uses createOrFirst plus an atomic guarded UPDATE, a renderable 409 exception keeps the controller tiny, and its tests are the strongest, including simulated races. But it inserts the child row before locking the coupon row. On InnoDB the FK check then takes a shared lock on the coupon, and the follow-up UPDATE needs an exclusive one. Under the load the task describes, two users redeeming at once will deadlock, and one gets a 500. I worked this out from the code; there was no MySQL server to reproduce it. The cap, the once rule and the single event still hold, but this is a real bug in the focus area.

impl-1 and impl-3 lock the coupon row (FOR UPDATE) first. That serialises requests correctly and avoids the deadlock. Neither fixed the guest-without-JSON-Accept case, which returns a 500 instead of 401; impl-2 did fix it.

impl-1 keeps the logic on the model and uses route binding and whereBelongsTo, with a thin controller. Its weak spots are a nullable return used to mean 'used up' and writing the count back into $this.

impl-3 puts everything in a fat controller: a manual lookup with abort(404), abort(409) inside the transaction, a positional tuple return, and a mass-assignable redeemed_count.

Because real bugs weigh heavily, impl-1 ranks first. It is correct under concurrency and reasonably idiomatic. impl-2 is second: its craftsmanship is clearly better, but the likely deadlock in the focus area pulls it down. impl-3 is third: correct but the least idiomatic.
